item.title: Development of SELF and IDEAL body size perception in children aged 6–12 years
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Background: Several studies have investigated children’s body image using figure rating scales, and found females’ selection of IDEAL (ideal body image) was significantly thinner than SELF (perceived current body image) and males’ selection of IDEAL. However, no studies have investigated children’s body image using virtual reality avatars. This study examined whether the discrepancy between SELF and IDEAL is greater in female than in male children aged 6 to 12 years using photorealistic figure rating scales. Methods: Female and male photorealistic body size scales based on Body Mass Index (BMI) were created using MakeHuman and Blender, and children rated their SELF and IDEAL body images using these scales. Results: Discrepancy between SELF and IDEAL body image was present among younger female (6.3–8.5 years) and older (10.3–12.5 years) elementary school children, but not among middle elementary school children (8.3–10.5 years). Conclusion: These findings suggest that body dissatisfaction, similar to that observed in adult females, emerges or is already formed at an early age. Trial registration: Not applicable.

item.title: Exercise motivation profiles and their association with physical activity behavior and psychological wellbeing in Chinese adolescents: a latent profile analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Physical activity (PA) declines during adolescence, and insufficient PA is prevalent among Chinese youth. Motivation, as conceptualized within self-determination theory (SDT), is a central correlate of PA engagement, yet most studies have used variable-centered approaches that overlook how different behavioral regulations co-occur within individuals. Methods This cross-sectional study applied latent profile analysis (LPA) to the five Behavioral Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire-2 subscales in 856 adolescents (51.3% boys; M age = 15.0 years, SD = 1.7) recruited from six secondary schools in Changchun, China, who also completed the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form and the WHO-5 WellBeing Index. Profile differences in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and wellbeing were tested with the BCH three-step method, unadjusted and adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, and correlates of membership were examined with R3STEP. Results A four-profile solution was retained on the basis of the Bayesian information criterion: autonomous (32.5%), mixed (35.9%), controlled (21.4%), and amotivated (10.3%). MVPA and WHO-5 scores decreased monotonically across profiles; covariate-adjusted means ranged from 313.6 to 92.3 min/week for MVPA and from 16.80 to 10.23 for WHO-5, with Wald chi-square(3) equal to 109.683 and 137.27 respectively, both p less than 0.001. Older age, female sex, and higher BMI were associated with membership in the less autonomous profiles. Discussion Exercise motivation among Chinese adolescents is organized into person-centered profiles that differ systematically in self-reported PA and wellbeing. The design is cross-sectional and all measures were self-reported, so these associations are descriptive rather than causal, and whether profile-based screening improves outcomes remains untested.

item.title: Toward a Neurocognitive Account of CASA: EEG Evidence from Human and ChatGPT-Enabled Social Robot Conversation
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, this study compared electroencephalographic (EEG) responses during naturalistic conversation with a human interlocutor and Pepper 1.8a, a social robot powered by a customized ChatGPT API. Female university students in South Korea discussed merit- versus need-based scholarships with both interlocutors in a within-subjects experiment. Human interaction elicited higher frontal theta and higher central-parietal alpha power than robot interaction, which may indicate greater demands on interaction monitoring and adaptive control, as well as a different attentional-regulatory state, during human interaction. Frontal alpha asymmetry did not significantly differ between conditions, providing no evidence of a difference in approach-related motivational orientation. In exploratory analyses, greater frontal alpha asymmetry during human relative to robot interaction was associated with a smaller difference in enjoyment. These findings provide downstream neurophysiological evidence relevant to CASA: interaction with a social robot was associated with EEG responses linked to ongoing interaction-related processes.

item.title: Instructional self-talk outperforms motivational self-talk during competition: a multimethod examination of motor performance and verbal-analytic processing
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Instructional self-talk (IST) is typically more effective than motivational self-talk (MST) in supporting the execution of discrete precision-oriented motor skills during training. However, research has yet to examine whether previously observed differences between IST and MST persist during competitive conditions. Drawing from reinvestment theory, we hypothesized that IST would produce greater conscious motor processing, and that MST would produce performance outcomes that were no worse than, and potentially superior to, those of IST during competition. Design A multi-method, between-group design was used to directly compare IST and MST during a golf-putting competition. Method Forty participants completed 40 putts while internally reciting either IST cues (“ feet still – wrists locked – arms through ”) or MST cues (“ come on, I can do this ”). We measured putting accuracy, kinematics, self-reported conscious processing, and electroencephalographic (EEG) indices associated with verbal-analytic processing. Results Participants using IST hit putts closer to the target and demonstrated better technique than those using MST. Bayesian analyses revealed that the observed data for radial error, length error and lateral clubhead acceleration were, respectively, 1.51, 1.24 and 17.1 times more likely under the alternative hypothesis (group differences; IST superior to MST) than under the null hypothesis. Contrary to predictions, the data did not provide compelling evidence that IST elicited greater conscious processing or altered cortical dynamics compared with MST. Conclusion For discrete motor skills such as golf putting, brief and simple IST cues may provide notable technique advantages and modest performance advantages over MST during competition. Implication Brief and simple IST cues may help performers maintain goal-directed attention, facilitating effective movement execution and performance during competition.

item.title: Eye tracking in epilepsy: neurobiological rationale, clinical applications, and a translational research agenda
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Current clinical tools for epilepsy monitoring have well-defined limitations. Seizure diaries undercount non-convulsive events, cognitive screening lacks process-level resolution, and plasma drug monitoring reflects pharmacokinetic exposure rather than neural effects. Eye tracking provides a complementary approach by capturing oculomotor behavior that is continuously quantifiable, does not rely on patient self-report, and depends on cortical and subcortical circuits affected by epileptogenic pathology and antiseizure medications. This review examines eye tracking as a translational biomarker approach across four domains: cognitive phenotyping, pharmacodynamic monitoring, seizure semiology, and presurgical functional mapping, and grades the evidence maturity of each domain from discovery to clinical utility. Impaired antisaccade and other voluntary saccade performance is the most frequently replicated finding, reported in several small cohorts and in one recent single-center cohort of 442 adults. It is consistent with executive dysfunction that standard screening may miss, but it has not been validated externally, and current data cannot fully separate disease effects from medication effects. Saccade dynamics are an established pharmacodynamic marker in clinical pharmacology, but epilepsy-specific evidence is limited to one study comparing treated patients with controls, which did not measure plasma drug levels. In contrast, semiology quantification and presurgical applications remain at an early stage of development. The main barriers to clinical translation are methodological, with additional hardware constraints for ambulatory use. Existing studies are small, cross-sectional, and heterogeneous, with limited use of concurrent EEG during cognitive paradigms and inconsistent reporting of acquisition and preprocessing methods. Because similar oculomotor abnormalities occur in other neurological and psychiatric disorders, these measures are better viewed as transdiagnostic markers of network dysfunction than as epilepsy-specific biomarkers. Addressing these gaps requires standardized protocols, validated analysis pipelines, and longitudinal, multi-site study designs. Eye tracking is unlikely to replace existing clinical tools, but may extend their application by providing objective, process-level measures of neural function.

item.title: Psychological experiences and information needs of patients awaiting eligibility assessment for an implantable brain–computer interface in a clinical trial: a qualitative study
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Objective To explore the psychological experiences and information needs of patients awaiting eligibility assessment for an implantable brain–computer interface (BCI) and to provide a basis for developing targeted nursing interventions and health education strategies. Methods A descriptive phenomenological study analysed with Colaizzi (1978) seven-step method was conducted from March to May 2026 at a tertiary hospital in Beijing. Using purposive sampling, 12 patients awaiting eligibility assessment for an implantable brain–computer interface were recruited: 10 men and 2 women aged 35–60 years, with motor impairment attributable to stroke ( n = 7), spinal cord injury ( n = 3), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ( n = 1), or hyperphenylalaninemia ( n = 1). Semistructured, in-depth individual interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim in Mandarin, and analysed on the Chinese transcripts. Trustworthiness was addressed through reflexive bracketing, independent coding by two researchers with team-based resolution of discrepancies, an audit trail of analytic decisions, member checking, and reporting guided by the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ). Results The essential structure of the experience was a state of “suspended anticipation”: participants anchored their hopes for a better future in a technology they could not fully understand while simultaneously confronting the possibility that they would never reach it. Five interrelated themes described constituents of this experience: (1) positive expectations regarding treatment; (2) multifaceted concerns; (3) concurrent physical and psychological distress; (4) information gaps and unmet informational needs; and (5) coping responses and support needs. Hope and fear coexisted within the same participants rather than alternating between them. Conclusion Patients awaiting BCI eligibility assessment experienced a complex interplay of hope and anxiety, persistent physical and psychological distress, and resilience. They also reported limited access to reliable information, misconceptions regarding the eligibility assessment and treatment process, and diverse support needs. A coordinated support system integrating psychological care, tailored health education, ongoing follow-up, and family involvement may improve patients’ well-being, care experience, and engagement with the assessment and rehabilitation process.

item.title: Awareness-dependent Attentional Templates: Neural Mechanism Differentiation Driven by Visual Working Memory Load
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Visual working memory (VWM) guides attention via internal attentional templates, but whether this relies on a "single" or "multiple" templates and how awareness and VWM load regulate its neural mechanisms remain unclear. This study used a VWM-guided visual search paradigm with backward masking (awareness manipulation) and EEG. Behavioral results showed that aware VWM supported multi-template attention guidance, while subjectively unaware VWM only allowed single-template guidance. EEG revealed that alpha oscillations over posterior electrodes indexed attention allocation. Neural mechanisms differed by VWM load: Single-item maintenance relied on posterior alpha-alpha phase coupling, while multi-item maintenance depended on theta-alpha cross-frequency coupling between anterior and bilateral posterior regions. These findings clarify how awareness regulates VWM attentional template mode and reveal load-specific neural coupling, providing evidence for understanding working memory-attention-awareness interactions.

item.title: Patterns of Alpha-band Power Reflect Prioritization of the Most Recently Encoded Location in a Working Memory Sequence
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Space and time play a critical role in working memory formation and maintenance relative to other object features. Particularly, covert spatial attention spontaneously tracks object locations in working memory and is thought to enable feature binding at those location markers. However, whether object locations are attended concurrently as multiple objects are presented in a sequence remains a topic of debate. Here, we investigated whether spatial attention contributes to sustained active memory maintenance when items are separated in both space and time. We report two experiments that differed in whether color or location was the tested feature. In each experiment, we measured EEG alpha-band power while participants memorized the target feature of two sequentially presented colored dots. We then applied an inverted encoding model to the topography of oscillatory alpha-band power (8-12 Hz) on the scalp to measure how long the location of each item was attended. In Experiment 1, participants performed a delayed color estimation task, and we found that patterns of alpha-band power tracked the location of the most recently presented item. In Experiment 2, participants performed a delayed spatial estimation task, and we found that patterns of alpha-band power tracked the location of Item 1 for longer than observed in Experiment 1. However, only the most recently presented item (Item 2) sustained until the end of the delay. Taken together, our results show that, although both items need to be remembered, covert spatial attention prioritizes items one at a time when they are displayed in a sequence.

item.title: Data‐Driven EEG ‐ fMRI Fusion: From Multimodal Integration to Latent Neural Inference
item.description:
Human Brain Mapping
ABSTRACT Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) capture neural dynamics across complementary temporal and spatial scales, but analyzing them jointly is difficult: the two modalities differ in measurement mechanisms, temporal resolution, and neurovascular coupling. EEG‐fMRI fusion can be framed as an inverse problem, where the goal is to recover latent neural processes only partially observed through electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals. Here, we review data‐driven fusion methods published between 2000 and 2025, focusing on techniques that identify shared neural representations across modalities. We organize methods by fusion strategies (symmetric vs. asymmetric), methodological objectives (factorization vs. translation), and modeling assumptions (linear vs. nonlinear), and discuss evaluation metrics and visualization strategies in current use. A recurring finding is the absence of a universal validation standard and the difficulty of interpreting latent multimodal components. Across neurological, psychiatric, and cognitive applications, EEG‐fMRI fusion has revealed distributed network dynamics not accessible through unimodal analyses, though temporal misalignment, noise‐induced coupling, and model‐dependent interpretation remain persistent challenges. We close by discussing directions including nonlinear modeling, flexible coupling frameworks, and large‐scale group‐level fusion, and situate the field within a broader view of EEG‐fMRI fusion as a problem of latent neural inference.

item.title: Effects of Digital Human on Cross-Cultural User Experience and Learning Outcomes in IVR Architectural Heritage Games
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Immersive virtual reality (IVR) offers new paradigms for cross-cultural interpretation of architectural heritage, yet how IVR game guidance modes affect user experience and learning across cultures remains underexplored. This study investigated the effects of guidance mode (digital human guide vs. voice-over guide) on user experience, learning outcomes, flow, and cognitive load in an IVR architectural heritage game, with cultural background (native vs. non-native) as a moderator. Eighty-one participants were randomly assigned to two conditions in a 2 × 2 between-subjects design. Multimodal data included questionnaires, physiological measures (electrodermal activity, EDA; heart rate, HR; heart rate variability, HRV, electroencephalography, EEG), and interviews. Results showed that the digital human guide yielded better learning outcomes and enhanced neurophysiological flow, whereas the voice-over guide may yield higher subjective satisfaction. Cultural background may moderate cognitive load at the neural level. Importantly, physiological measures captured effects undetected by subjective reports, highlighting the necessity of multimodal assessment in cross-cultural immersive heritage research.

item.title: Associations Between Long-Term High-Altitude Exposure and Cognitive Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Studies on Event-Related Potentials
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Although long-term high-altitude (HA) exposure is associated with cognitive alterations, evidence regarding the corresponding event-related potential (ERP) components is inconsistent, and a systematic synthesis across processing stages is lacking. This meta-analysis synthesized available ERP evidence to examine neurophysiological alterations associated with cognitive processing following long-term HA exposure. The most consistent finding was a reduction in P300 amplitude among the HA groups (g = −0.476). Reduced P100 amplitude was also observed (g = −0.325), although this finding was less robust, with a possible small-study-effect signal. Rotation-related negativity amplitude was more negative in HA groups (g = −0.748), but this estimate was based on only four independent studies. No reliable between-group differences were observed for other evaluated ERP outcomes. Moderator analyses provided limited evidence of systematic moderation and are constrained by low statistical power. Overall, the available evidence is heterogeneous and primarily based on cross-sectional comparisons. These findings suggest possible stage-dependent associations between long-term HA exposure and ERP alterations, although rigorous longitudinal studies using standardized ERP protocols are needed to substantiate these associations.

item.title: Neurocognitive effects of internal and external attention training in adolescents: insights from Indian yogic practices
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Adolescence with its rapid development of cognitive processes and reorganization of brain networks serves as an important age group for studying the impact of cognitive training-based interventions. Traditional Indian mind–body practices such as Yoga Nidra (YN) and Trataka have shown promising impact on cognitive enhancement, although their combined effects and mechanistic underpinnings remain largely unexplored. Therefore, the current study aimed to investigate the effects of a combined YN and Trataka intervention on cognitive performance and resting state (RS) EEG activities of adolescents. Methods Typically developing, school going adolescents ( N = 27) aged 14–16 years were selected from the southern part of India, who underwent 10 weeks of intervention. Relevant cognitive (attention, executive function, processing speed, visuospatial processing and working memory) and RS-EEG (both eyes closed and opened conditions) measures were obtained at baseline, 4 weeks and 10 weeks of intervention. Suitable parametric and non-parametric measures were employed to examine time-dependent effects, along with post-hoc comparisons. Results Significant improvement in performance was observed across all domains of cognition ( p < 0.001), with most substantial improvement after the initial 4 weeks of intervention, and more stable and sustained long-term effects post 10 weeks. Although RS-EEG measures did not show statistically significant differences across times, but in the closed eyes condition, a trend of an increasing alpha power (0.54 at baseline, 0.60 at 4 weeks and 0.62 at 10 weeks) and decreasing beta power (0.24 at baseline, 0.19 at 4 weeks and 0.17 at 10 weeks) was observed, suggesting enhanced cognitive efficiency. Conclusion The patterns of early gains and sustained impact of the combined YN and Trataka intervention highlight its potential to support cognitive enhancement in adolescents, although the results are from a single-arm exploratory study. Future randomized controlled trials are required for establishing causal influences of the practices. Moreover, this also serves as a scalable and culturally grounded practice which can be integrated into modern school settings.

item.title: Human or Not? Prior Knowledge, Recognition of Virtual Identity, and Neural and Subjective Responses to a Hyperrealistic Virtual Influencer
item.description:
Cyberpsychology Behavior and Social Networking
Despite the growing popularity of virtual social media influencers (VIs), little is known about how knowledge and recognition of a VI's virtual identity are associated with neural and subjective responses. We investigated whether prior knowledge of virtual identity, recognition during viewing, or remaining unaware was associated with differences in brain activity and subjective evaluations. Twenty female college students viewed a 1-minute silent video featuring a hyperrealistic Korean virtual influencer while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded. Subsequently, participants completed subjective evaluations and retrospectively reported prior knowledge or recognition of the influencer's virtual identity. Exploratory analyses compared EEG changes from eyes-closed rest and five subjective evaluation composite scores across the three groups, with correction for multiple comparisons. After correction for multiple comparisons, neither the EEG analyses nor the subjective composite analyses yielded statistically significant group differences. Descriptive means varied across groups, but these imprecisely estimated patterns did not establish group differences. The findings underscore the methodological importance of distinguishing prior knowledge from recognition during viewing. Computers Are Social Actors and Uncanny Valley perspectives generate hypotheses for future time-resolved studies rather than mechanisms demonstrated by the present data.

item.title: Exploring attentional bias in posttraumatic stress disorder: insights from police officers with service dogs
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction PTSD is characterized by hypervigilance and attentional bias to threat, which can severely interfere with daily functioning. Stress exacerbates this bias by increasing amygdala activity and depleting prefrontal resources, reducing attentional control. The presence of a dog may help regulate attention by reducing stress. Methods This study investigates attentional bias to emotional faces in police officers with PTSD and examines whether the presence of their service or companion dog diminishes this bias by mitigating stress-related cognitive depletion, using a within subject design. Police officers with ( n = 24) and without PTSD ( n = 24) completed the dot-probe task with angry and happy faces in the presence and absence of their dog. Reaction times and event-related potentials (ERP) were analyzed to assess attentional bias. Results Officers with PTSD showed a greater trial level bias score but no consistent bias direction. The P3 amplitude indicated no differentiation between happy and angry faces in the PTSD group, unlike the control group. The VPP amplitude was higher in the PTSD group when the dog was absent, suggesting increased early-stage attention to faces without the dog. Officers with PTSD showed also slower reaction times when their dog was absent. Discussion The findings suggest that PTSD is associated with a reduced ability to selectively allocate attention based on emotional content and increased reaction time variability rather than a consistent directional bias toward or away from emotional stimuli. The presence of a dog appeared to regulate early-stage attentional processing and reaction speed.

item.title: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user’s own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR–electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

item.title: Perceived weight status, body image, and depressive symptoms in Korean adolescents: a three-wave longitudinal study and within-person analysis
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Body dissatisfaction is a well-established risk factor for adolescent depression, but two questions remain open. First, it is unclear whether perceived weight status—a subjective cognitive appraisal of one’s body—relates to body image and depression differently from objective body size. Second, most longitudinal evidence relies on between-person models that cannot isolate within-person change. Drawing on a cognitive-behavioral model of body image, we distinguish perceived weight status (a perceptual-categorical appraisal) from body image (the attitudinal-evaluative dimension) and examine both between- and within-person processes. We analyzed three-wave longitudinal data from the Panel Study on Korean Children (ages 13–15; analytic N = 1,148–1,304). A temporally ordered mediation model (perceived weight status at Wave 14 → body image at Wave 15 → depressive symptoms at Wave 16) was estimated using structural equation modeling, controlling for prior depressive symptoms and sex-standardized BMI. Indirect effects were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap resamples with bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals. We examined within-person dynamics using two- and three-variable random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs). Body image was assessed using a refined 4-item scale (α = .735, ω = .77). Perceiving oneself as heavier at W14 predicted a less positive body image at W15 (β = −0.126, p < .001), which in turn predicted higher depressive symptoms at W16 (β = −0.101, p < .001), yielding a small but significant indirect effect (0.013, 95% BCa CI [0.005, 0.025]). Sex-standardized BMI did not significantly predict body image (β = −0.064, p = .091), but the coefficients for perceived weight status and BMI did not differ significantly (Δ = −0.062, p = .368). The indirect effect did not differ by sex (Δ = −0.003, p = .776), although the component paths did. In the RI-CLPM, perceived weight status showed no prospective within-person association with body image ( p = .135) or depressive symptoms ( p = .594). In contrast, body image and depressive symptoms were reciprocally associated within persons (both ps < .01), independent of stable between-person differences. Perceived weight status was prospectively associated with body image, while body image and depressive symptoms showed reciprocal within-person associations. However, the mediational pathway was not supported at the within-person level, suggesting that the observed indirect association may primarily reflect between-person differences. Prevention and intervention efforts may therefore benefit from targeting the reciprocal body image–depression cycle rather than assuming a unidirectional, perception-driven pathway.

item.title: The temporal representation of computational features from body expressions
item.description:
Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience
Body expression is an important channel for human communication. To understand the underlying perceptual mechanisms, the present study used electroencephalography and time-resolved multivariate analyses to track the temporal emergence of computationally defined body features and their contribution to emotion representations. Six body postural features (i.e. limb angles, symmetry, shoulder ratio, surface, potential energy, and limb contraction) were computed based on 14 body joints. Representational similarity analysis revealed that the body surface and potential energy were significantly encoded at an early stage, persisting for an extended duration over parietal-posterior electrodes. In contrast, limb contraction was encoded at a later stage and exhibited a shorter duration. Furthermore, commonality analysis demonstrated that the postural features of surface and potential energy explained the neural variance of emotion categories, with body surface accounting for the largest proportion of the shared neural variance. These findings provide empirical evidence for the temporal dynamics of computationally defined body-posture representations during emotional body perception and may inform future computational models of body expression perception.

item.title: Electroencephalography neurophysiology alterations in association with Aβ and tau pathology across the symptomatic stages of Alzheimer’s disease continuum: a cross-sectional study
item.description:
NeuroImage
BACKGROUND: Amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau deposition drive Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, how these proteinopathies are linked to macroscopic neural activity alterations measured by electroencephalography (EEG) in symptomatic AD remains inadequately characterized. This study aims to investigate the associations between Aβ, tau, EEG neurophysiology, and cognition. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 73 MCI and AD participants, who underwent resting-state EEG, Aβ-PET, and tau-PET. EEG source analysis was performed to extract regional spectral power. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the associations of regional Aβ (quantified by SUVR), tau (binary classification), with EEG features, controlling for age, sex and education. Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression was applied to investigate the relationships of EEG spectral power and global Aβ burden with cognitive performance. RESULTS: Elevated Aβ burden was associated with distinct regional spectral alterations. Specifically, higher Aβ SUVR was significantly correlated with increased theta power and decreased beta power in a subset of cortical regions. Tau positivity did not modulate the amyloid-theta association in any region, but attenuated the amyloid-beta association in a small set of parietal regions. CONCLUSIONS: We identified a localized pattern of Aβ-related neurophysiological dysfunction across the symptomatic stages of AD continuum, characterized by theta increases and beta decreases, supporting a robust association between Aβ burden and cortical neural slowing. The findings highlight the value of source-localized EEG power as a sensitive indicator of Aβ-associated network dysfunction in AD and underscore the potential of source-localized EEG as a complementary, non-invasive biomarker for assessing pathological burden and informing diagnostic strategies in AD.

item.title: Meditation as a bioactive intervention: evidence of translational potential via Connectivity Mapping and TMS neurophysiology
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Abstract Meditation practices are often used as non-pharmacological adjunct therapy for managing stress and well-being benefits. We propose that beneath their non-pharmacological facade, meditation practices might operate via drug target modulation having profound neurophysiological effects. Firstly, we leverage the Connectivity Map (CMap) to investigate (a) the overlap between meditation-induced molecular signatures and established drug responses, and (b) the pathways and mechanisms contributing to meditation’ potential therapeutic effects. This was studied in a comprehensive temporal RNAseq dataset comprising premeditation, meditation, and follow-up stages from a clinical trial involving 106 participants practising inner engineering meditation. Meditation signatures overlapped with over 438 drugs, but predominantly with drugs targeting the neuroactive ligand receptor pathways, capable of modulating the brain’s excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance. Next, to bridge the meditation-induced molecular changes to measurable neurophysiological effects, we performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of drugs affecting E/I balance through the lens of non-invasive brain stimulation, i.e., transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS-EMG and TMS-EEG). Using multiple correspondence analysis, we then clustered the CMap informed neuroactive drugs and their E/I effects on the same latent space. We found that meditation’s effects mimic drugs targeting the GABAergic, Glutametergic and other neuromodulatory system pathways. Our findings lead to a working model to objectively test neurophysiological changes resulting from meditation that can lead to evidence-based clinical applications. Overall, these findings support the view that meditation acts as a biologically active intervention capable of modulating molecular pathways and cortical excitability, rather than functioning solely as a psychological or contemplative practice.

item.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958–0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Digital meditation at scale: a randomized citizen science trial comparing four meditation practices
item.description:
BMC Psychology
This preregistered randomized controlled trial evaluated whether app-delivered meditation improved psychological, cognitive, and physiological outcomes relative to an active control, whether four meditation techniques differed in their effects, and whether individual differences moderated response. A total of 1,211 adults were randomized to four weeks of app-guided loving-kindness, mantra, body scan, or nondual meditation, or to a classical-music active control. Self-report (well-being, mood, self-transcendence, nondual awareness, interoception, compassion), cognitive (Stroop, N-back), and physiological (electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate variability (HRV), heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEP)) outcomes were assessed before and after the intervention and analyzed with linear mixed models and false-discovery-rate correction. No preregistered meditation-versus-control outcome survived FDR correction, and Bayes factors additionally favored the null for the temporal EEG measures. None of the four preregistered technique-specific hypotheses was supported. Two self-report outcomes showed arm differences surviving correction on non-predicted contrasts (self-compassion isolation and sleep quality, both q = 0.050), and mantra participants showed faster working-memory reaction time than body scan participants. The four techniques did not differ from one another. In exploratory moderation analyses, trait neuroticism moderated the meditation effect on working-memory reaction time, with higher-neuroticism participants showing greater benefit in cognitive speed than controls. Four weeks of app-based meditation was not superior to an active music control across psychological, cognitive, and physiological measures, and no preregistered technique-specific hypothesis was supported. The neuroticism finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants replication. Endpoint data were available for 43% of randomized participants and missingness was non-random, which limits inference. This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/xdjfq/overview) on October 24, 2024. International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number, ISRCTN10867561, retrospectively registered on August​ 12, 2026.
